700.title: [RFC]Integrate Intel Extension for Pytorch into accelerate to get out-of-box optimizations on intel platform.
700.body:
### Motivation
Intel Extension for Pytorch(a.k.a IPEX) can provides extra optimization and performance boost on intel hardware platform(currently only for CPU) for both inference and training. These optimization include graph level optimization such as operator fusion, auto mixed precision which support rich bf16 operators and optimization for optimizer which boost the training performance. In contrast with trainer, accelerate mostly is used with distributed training and inference on transformer model, but it also can benefit from IPEX's optimization. So, integrate IPEX into accelerate can make users who do distributed training or evaluation get out-of-box performance boost on CPU.

### Design
#### User interface

- The first thing is how we tell accelerate to enable ipex. We can utilize the CLI tool **accelerate config** to config our training and inference environment with IPEX feature enabled. This tool will ask a series of questions including IPEX related config such as _ipex_enabled_ and _ipex_fusion_enabled_.  We can also pass these two options to our python script which is launched by **accelerate launch**. The detailed usage examples of these two scenarios can refer to [user-12's comments](https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/issues/700#issuecomment-1247766735).
The meaning of these two option:
ipex_enabled: If this option is set, the IPEX's python package will be imported, and optimization such as Conv+BN folding and [weight prepacking](https://intel.github.io/intel-extension-for-pytorch/latest/tutorials/api_doc.html) will at least be applied at inference.
ipex_fusion_enabled: Besides the basic optimization, operator fusion is also an important technic to boost the performance, we can trace a model to enable this graph level optimization first, and then ipex will provide more specially optimized fusion op on intel platform with this option.

- Model and optimizer wrapper for distributed training. 
```
model, optim, data = accelerator.prepare(model, optim, data)
```
Accelerator.prepare() is the main method where most magic happens, IPEX can also hide optimization via a similar front end API called ipex.optimize(). If we choose use ipex, then we can automatically invoke ipex's API inside prepare(). If the current workload is training, the still use the original accelerate's original prepare API like this: **model, optim, data = accelerator.prepare(model, optim, data)**  ,so, there is no code change in training. But for inference, if we want to benefit from ipex's optimization in addition to operator fusion such as [weight prepack](https://intel.github.io/intel-extension-for-pytorch/1.11.200/tutorials/api_doc.html) etc, we must explicit pass model to prepare method such as:
```
data = accelerator.prepare(data) # Origin evaluation
model, data = accelerator.prepare(model, data) # Need explicitly pass model to prepare() to benefit from broader ipex's optimization. 
```

4249.title: prepare_model unconditionally imports DTensor, breaking single-GPU training on torch builds without a distributed backend
4249.body:
### What happens

`Accelerator.prepare_model` calls `model_has_dtensor(model)` while computing `device_placement`. That function imports `torch.distributed.tensor`, which transitively imports `torch._C._distributed_c10d`. On a PyTorch build compiled without a distributed backend, the import raises and every single-GPU run dies at trainer start.

AMD's official Windows ROCm wheels (`repo.amd.com/rocm/whl/...`) are such a build: `torch.distributed` imports, but `torch.distributed.is_available()` is `False` and `torch._C._distributed_c10d` does not exist. This currently breaks all training on AMD GPUs on Windows.

### Reproduction

```python
import torch, torch.nn as nn, accelerate
from accelerate import Accelerator

print("accelerate", accelerate.__version__)
print("has _distributed_c10d:", hasattr(torch._C, "_distributed_c10d"))
print("torch.distributed.is_available():", torch.distributed.is_available())

Accelerator().prepare_model(nn.Linear(4, 4))
print("PASS")
```

On `torch 2.11.0+rocm7.13.0` (Windows 11, Python 3.13), same machine, only the accelerate version differs:

```
accelerate 1.14.0
has _distributed_c10d: False
torch.distributed.is_available(): False
PASS

accelerate 1.15.0
has _distributed_c10d: False
torch.distributed.is_available(): False
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'torch._C._distributed_c10d'; 'torch._C' is not a package
```

Trimmed traceback on 1.15.0:

```
  accelerate/accelerator.py:1802   in prepare_model     -> and not model_has_dtensor(model)
  accelerate/utils/other.py:243    in model_has_dtensor -> from torch.distributed.tensor import DTensor
  torch/distributed/tensor/__init__.py:4
  torch/distributed/tensor/_ops/_conv_ops.py:5
  torch/distributed/tensor/_dtensor_spec.py:9
  torch/distributed/tensor/placement_types.py:10
  torch/distributed/_functional_collectives.py:9
  torch/distributed/distributed_c10d.py:25 -> from torch._C._distributed_c10d import (...)
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'torch._C._distributed_c10d'; 'torch._C' is not a package
```

### Where it regressed

In v1.14.0 the only `model_has_dtensor(model)` call is at `accelerator.py:1878`, guarded by:

```python
if self.multi_device and not (self.parallelism_config and self.parallelism_config.tp_enabled):
```

so a single-GPU run never reached it.

v1.15.0 adds a second, unguarded call at `accelerator.py:1802`, inside the `device_placement` computation that every `prepare_model` executes. That appears to come from #4181 (`f7cc8e9a57993e049d21f2755fa85d3afc17af7b`, merged 2026-09-03), first released in 1.15.0 on 2026-09-09.

### Suggested fix

Either short-circuit `model_has_dtensor` when `torch.distributed.is_available()` is `False`, or restore the multi-device guard on the new call site. The first looks more robust, since a DTensor cannot be present at all without a distributed build.

Related, previously accepted as a supported configuration: #1787.

### Environment

- accelerate 1.15.0 (fails) / 1.14.0 (works)
- torch 2.11.0+rocm7.13.0, W

4306.title: split_between_processes crashes on tuples when apply_padding=True
4306.body:
`split_between_processes` documents `tuple` as an accepted input type, but combining it with `apply_padding=True` raises a TypeError on every rank:

```
TypeError: can only concatenate tuple (not "list") to tuple
```

The padding gets concatenated to `result` as a list, but `result` is a tuple slice, and `tuple += list` fails even when there is nothing to pad, so this fails no matter how the data divides up.

Repro with `torchrun --nproc_per_node=2`:

```python
from accelerate.state import PartialState

state = PartialState(cpu=True)
with state.split_between_processes((1, 2, 3), apply_padding=True) as out:
    print(out)
```

Lists work fine, tuples die on both ranks. Seen on main (1.16.0.dev0) with torch 2.5.1, on CPU and CUDA.

4226.title: find_executable_batch_size does not catch MPS out-of-memory errors
4226.body:
`find_executable_batch_size` re-raises on the first MPS out-of-memory error instead of lowering the batch size.

`should_reduce_batch_size` (`src/accelerate/utils/memory.py`, lines 108 to 116) matches on `" out of memory."`, with a trailing period. The MPS allocator raises:

```
RuntimeError: MPS backend out of memory (MPS allocated: 0 bytes, other allocations: 448.00 KiB, max allowed: 242.48 MiB). Tried to allocate 256.00 MiB on shared pool. Use PYTORCH_MPS_HIGH_WATERMARK_RATIO=0.0 to disable upper limit for memory allocations (may cause system failure).
```

"out of memory" is followed by " (" rather than ".", so no statement matches and the decorator re-raises. The message has been the same since at least torch v2.1.0 (`aten/src/ATen/mps/MPSAllocator.mm`), and it is a plain `RuntimeError`, not `torch.OutOfMemoryError`.

### Reproduction

accelerate 1.15.0.dev0 at 9e5d1de, torch 2.14.0, macOS arm64, Python 3.13. The watermark ratio makes the allocator refuse anything above about 240 MiB, so the OOM fires without filling the GPU.

```python
# repro.py, following the pattern in docs/source/basic_tutorials/troubleshooting.md
import sys, torch
from accelerate import Accelerator
from accelerate.utils import find_executable_batch_size

use_cpu = "--cpu" in sys.argv
accelerator = Accelerator(cpu=use_cpu)
unit = 2**25 if not use_cpu else 2**44  # 32 MiB per sample on MPS; 16 TiB per sample on CPU
tried = []

@find_executable_batch_size(starting_batch_size=32)
def inner(batch_size):
    tried.append(batch_size)
    accelerator.free_memory()
    x = torch.empty(batch_size * unit, dtype=torch.uint8, device=accelerator.device)
    return x.numel() // unit

print("device:", accelerator.device)
try:
    print("succeeded with batch_size =", inner())
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("raised", type(e).__name__ + ":", str(e)[:120])
print("batch sizes tried:", tried)
```

```
$ PYTORCH_MPS_HIGH_WATERMARK_RATIO=0.02 PYTORCH_MPS_LOW_WATERMARK_RATIO=0.01 python repro.py
device: mps
raised RuntimeError: MPS backend out of memory (MPS allocated: 0 bytes, other allocations: 448.00 KiB, max allowed: 242.48 MiB). Tried to all
batch sizes tried: [32]

$ python repro.py --cpu
device: cpu
succeeded with batch_size = 3
batch sizes tried: [32, 28, 25, 22, 19, 17, 15, 13, 11, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3]
```

The CPU allocator's message (`DefaultCPUAllocator: can't allocate memory`) is matched and the batch size steps down. On MPS the first failure propagates.

`tests/test_memory_utils.py` does not catch this. `raise_fake_out_of_memory` raises `f"{torch_device.upper()} out of memory."`, which on an MPS host is `"MPS out of memory."` and matches the `" out of memory."` statement. The real allocator message does not.

### Expected behavior

The batch size steps down on MPS the way it does on CPU and CUDA.

`transformers.Trainer` with `auto_find_batch_size=True` delegates to this function through `trainer_utils.find_executable_batch_size`, so that option cannot recover from an OOM on

4111.title: concatenate() still raises TypeError on non-tensor batch fields when num_processes > 1
4111.body:
### Context

#3849 reported that `DataLoaderDispatcher` (used when `dispatch_batches=True`, the default for an `IterableDataset`) crashed on non-tensor batch values (str/bool/list) returned by a data collator. 

#3850 fixed the single-process case by adding a `len(data) == 1` short-circuit in `concatenate()`:
```python
elif isinstance(data[0], torch.Tensor):
    return torch.cat(data, dim=dim)
elif isinstance(data, (tuple, list)) and len(data) == 1:
    return data[0]
else:
    raise TypeError(f"Can only concatenate tensors but got {type(data[0])}")
```

### The remaining bug

`DataLoaderDispatcher._fetch_batches` gathers exactly `num_processes` raw batches before calling `concatenate`:
```python
for _ in range(self.state.num_processes):
    self._update_state_dict()
    batches.append(next(iterator))
batch = concatenate(batches, dim=0)
```

As soon as `num_processes > 1` and a batch field isn't a tensor, `concatenate()` still raises the exact same `TypeError` as before #3850.

The PR review discussion already covers this exact gap, but it's easy to miss since it's buried in review comments on a merged PR rather than tracked as an open issue: https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/pull/3850#discussion_r2560098952
>  @maintainer-1: "This is a fix that only works when we have one gpu (only one batch is passed in concatenate). The issue happens when we have multi-gpu..."
>
> @user-62: "The suggestion here works fine with single-process, but the len(data) is simply equal to the number of processes. In short: it'll always fail in multi-process settings."
>
> @user-62 (final): "Agreed, it's a step in the right direction, even though multi-process support is not possible... Not supporting IterableDataset + MultiGPU is a bit annoying."

So this is a confirmed, intentional trade-off, not an oversight. I'm opening this mainly so it's trackable/discoverable outside the PR thread.

### Minimal repro
```python
from accelerate.utils.operations import concatenate
import torch

data = [
    {"input_ids": torch.tensor([[1, 2]]), "label": True},
    {"input_ids": torch.tensor([[3, 4]]), "label": False},
]
concatenate(data)
# TypeError: Can only concatenate tensors but got <class 'bool'>
```

### Ask
@maintainer-1 mentioned in review: "We can add in the docstring that if we receive only one batch of data, we will return it as it." The current docstring says "If there is only a single batch of data, it is returned as-is," but doesn't spell out that non-tensor fields remain broken for num_processes > 1 on any Accelerate version. Could that be made explicit, so downstream library authors don't assume #3850 was a general fix? 

We hit exactly that assumption gap in `trl` KTOTrainer, where a collator returned a bool field as a plain list, fine for `num_processes == 1` (where CI happened to pass on latest Accelerate), broken for real multi-process streaming eval on any Accelerate version. 4277.title: `simple_launcher` discards the child's error, unlike the elastic launch path
4277.body:
### System Info

```
accelerate 1.12.0, and unchanged on main at b795b4838eb33bde60eb398649c4ab006874e3e9
```

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [X] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] One of the scripts in the examples/ folder of Accelerate or an officially supported `no_trainer` script in the `examples` folder of the `transformers` repo (such as `run_no_trainer_glue.py`)
- [X] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction

`simple_launcher` runs the training script with `subprocess.Popen` and, on a non-zero exit, raises a `CalledProcessError` built from the return code and the command alone: https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/blob/b795b4838eb33bde60eb398649c4ab006874e3e9/src/accelerate/commands/launch.py#L992-L1001

The child's stderr is inherited rather than read, and neither `output` nor `stderr` is passed to the exception, so a caller that catches it learns only that something exited non-zero.

```python
import subprocess
import sys

from accelerate.commands.launch import launch_command, launch_command_parser

args = launch_command_parser().parse_args(["--cpu", "--num_processes", "1", sys.argv[1]])
try:
    launch_command(args)
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
    print(f"parent sees : {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
    print(f"e.stderr    : {e.stderr!r}")
    print(f"e.output    : {e.output!r}")
```

The multi-process path already solves this. `multi_gpu_launcher` delegates to `torch.distributed.run`, and torch elastic propagates the child's root exception to the parent through error files, so the parent raises a `ChildFailedError` carrying the child's traceback in a "Root Cause" section.     def autocast(self):

        ```python

        >>> accelerator = Accelerator(mixed_precision="fp16")

        """
        if self.native_amp:
            if self.mixed_precision == "fp16" and is_torch_version(">=", "1.10"):
                autocast_context = torch.cuda.amp.autocast(dtype=torch.float16)
